title: Predictive variational inference: Learn the predictively optimal posterior distribution
one_liner: Learn an updated belief over model settings by optimizing predictive accuracy directly, instead of trying to mimic the Bayesian posterior when the model itself may be wrong.
lead: Variational inference usually finds a posterior distribution, which is an approximate updated belief about unknown model settings after data, by staying close to the Bayesian posterior defined by the model. That objective assumes the model is correctly specified. In practice the model can be wrong: the data-generating process may have extra heterogeneity, missing mechanisms, or incorrect likelihood assumptions. This paper asks a different question. Instead of matching the model-defined posterior, can we choose a belief over settings whose posterior predictive distribution, which is the distribution of future data implied by that belief, gives the best predictions under explicit scoring rules? Predictive variational inference answers yes and treats that learned belief as the target object.

problem.h2: A correct Bayesian posterior can still be the wrong target under model misspecification
paras: Bayesian inference is internally coherent once you choose a prior and a likelihood, which is the rule that says how likely the observed data are under one setting of the unknown values. Variational inference usually tries to approximate the resulting posterior efficiently. That is sensible only if the chosen model family is good enough that its posterior captures the uncertainty we actually care about.

But real models are often misspecified. They may force one parameter, which is one unknown setting of the model, to represent a population that actually contains subgroups, or they may use a likelihood that cannot express the tails or dependencies in the data. In those cases, the exact Bayesian posterior is faithful to the wrong model. The paper therefore optimizes the predictive consequences directly rather than treating posterior approximation itself as the final goal.

callout.html: Choose the variational posterior by asking which updated belief yields the best future-data predictions under proper scoring rules, because predictive quality can remain informative even when the model is imperfect.

steps.b: Choose a model and a variational family
steps.text: Start with the same ingredients as ordinary variational inference: a prior, a likelihood, and a tractable family of approximate beliefs.
Use each candidate variational belief to induce predictions for future or held-out data.
Apply proper scoring rules so the objective rewards predictive distributions that place probability on the outcomes that actually occur.

steps.b: Optimize the variational belief for prediction
steps.text: Adjust the belief until its predictive distribution scores best, even if that belief does not match the Bayesian posterior.
Use the resulting spread to detect whether one fixed parameter setting is inadequate for the population.

paras: The paper changes the optimization target. Ordinary variational inference aims to approximate the Bayesian posterior of the chosen model. Predictive variational inference aims to find the variational belief whose induced predictions are best under a scoring rule.

hidden.name: predictive adequacy of the learned belief
paras: The hidden quantity is predictive adequacy: how well the learned belief supports accurate and well-calibrated predictions for data that the model has not yet seen. This is different from closeness to the Bayesian posterior. A belief can be close to that posterior and still predict poorly if the underlying model family misses important structure.

PVI focuses on this quantity by evaluating each candidate belief through the predictive distribution it induces. If a slightly broader or shifted belief yields predictions that score better on new data, the method prefers it. That preference can also expose hidden heterogeneity, because a broader belief may be the only way for a misspecified model to account for diverse subpopulations.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark cases where prediction-focused uncertainty gives information that posterior approximation alone can miss.

reads.html: The method asks which learned belief gives the most trustworthy predictions, not which belief most faithfully copies the posterior of a possibly wrong model.

Predictive variational inference chooses the variational posterior by minimizing predictive scoring-rule loss, so the target is the predictively optimal posterior rather than the Bayesian posterior itself.

mechanism.h2: Why optimizing predictive scores changes the result
paras: The main mechanism is that predictions are downstream of the posterior, not identical to it. Standard variational inference inherits every modeling assumption built into the posterior target. If those assumptions are wrong, a closer posterior approximation simply reproduces the wrong target more faithfully because it is still optimizing toward the same flawed model-defined answer.

PVI breaks that chain by judging candidate beliefs through future-data performance. A belief that spreads mass across several parameter regions may predict better than the ordinary posterior because it compensates for unmodeled heterogeneity or incorrect noise assumptions. The method therefore behaves like an implicit model expansion: it uses extra uncertainty in the variational belief to absorb misspecification that the original model could not express directly.

This also explains the diagnostic value of the learned uncertainty. If prediction keeps improving only when the variational belief stays broader than the standard posterior, that is evidence that the model's one-parameter description is too narrow for the population it is trying to explain.

stages.s: Chosen prior, likelihood, and variational family
Map each candidate belief to a predictive distribution
Update the belief using the predictive score, because score-improving updates shift probability toward beliefs that match future outcomes more closely
Predictively optimal variational posterior and its uncertainty pattern

math.words: Choose the variational belief that minimizes predictive loss under a scoring rule. The score is computed on the posterior predictive distribution, not on closeness to the Bayesian posterior.
math.equation: best_q = argmin over q of predictive_score(predictive_distribution_induced_by_q, observed_data)
symbols: one candidate variational belief over the unknown values
the future-data distribution obtained by averaging model predictions under q
a proper scoring rule that rewards accurate and calibrated predictions
the variational belief chosen by predictive variational inference

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose two candidate variational beliefs both fit the observed data reasonably well.
Belief A is narrow and predicts that tomorrow's outcome will almost certainly be near one value.
Belief B is broader and assigns nontrivial probability to two plausible outcome ranges.
If the next observations repeatedly fall into both ranges, Belief B gets the better predictive score.
PVI therefore chooses Belief B even if Belief A would be closer to the model's ordinary Bayesian posterior.
The learned extra spread is informative because it signals that the model needed more predictive flexibility.

math.note: The equation is shorthand for the paper's full formulation, but it captures the decisive change: optimize prediction quality, not posterior imitation.

charts.title: Ordinary variational inference
charts.note: This method is internally consistent with the model, but it can stay overconfident when the model family is too narrow.

charts.title: Predictive variational inference
charts.note: The method can depart from the ordinary posterior because predictive scoring rewards beliefs that compensate for model error when doing so improves future-data prediction.

items.html: If the dataset is too small, a prediction-focused objective can be noisy because the method may chase accidental patterns in the observed outcomes instead of stable predictive structure.

items.b: The variational family can still be too limited.
items.html: PVI cannot represent a stronger predictive belief if the chosen variational family is too rigid to express the necessary spread or asymmetry, because the optimizer cannot select a shape that the family itself does not allow.

items.b: Prediction is not the only possible goal.
items.html: If a user needs parameter interpretation more than forecasting quality, moving away from the ordinary Bayesian posterior may be undesirable because the learned belief is optimized for prediction first.

The framework is most valuable when the model is an approximation to reality and the real objective is forecasting or decision support, because then predictive quality is the quantity that deserves direct optimization.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple regression problem where the data come from a mixture of two subpopulations but the fitted model assumes only one shared parameter. Compare ordinary variational inference with predictive variational inference on held-out predictions.

The demo should inspect both the forecast quality and the learned uncertainty. If PVI is working as claimed, it should keep a belief that predicts held-out outcomes better and that remains wider or more structured than the ordinary posterior because that extra spread is compensating for misspecification.
demo.closing: The central result is that the learned belief may move away from the Bayesian posterior and still be the right answer for prediction, because posterior imitation is no longer the objective.
